solution.why_correct: A missense mutation is a base substitution that results in a codon specifying a different amino acid than originally intended in the protein sequence; depending on the specific amino acid change and its position, this can potentially alter the protein's structure and/or function to varying degrees.
solution.why_others_wrong: Always resulting in a premature stop codon describes a specific type of nonsense mutation, not a missense mutation (which specifically results in a different AMINO ACID being specified, not a stop signal); a missense mutation, by definition, DOES typically change the amino-acid sequence (contrary to having absolutely no effect), though the functional significance of this change can vary; missense mutations can occur in the DNA/genes of cellular organisms generally (like the classic sickle cell anaemia example in humans), not being restricted only to RNA viruses.
solution.concept_recap: The sickle cell anaemia mutation, where a single missense mutation changes one amino acid in the beta-globin protein, is a classic, well-studied example illustrating the potentially significant functional consequences of a missense mutation.

ncertRef: NCERT Class 12, Ch. 6 (Molecular Basis of Inheritance)

question: Which of the following best describes a 'nonsense mutation,' as a specific, often severely disruptive outcome of certain point mutations?
options: A base substitution that changes a codon specifying an amino acid into a premature stop codon, resulting in a truncated (shortened), often non-functional protein
A mutation that has no effect on protein length or function
A mutation that only ever occurs at the very end of a gene's coding sequence
A mutation that always increases a protein's total length beyond normal

solution.why_correct: A nonsense mutation is a base substitution that converts a codon originally specifying an amino acid into a premature stop codon; this causes translation to terminate early, resulting in a shortened (truncated) protein that is often non-functional, especially if the mutation occurs early in the coding sequence.
solution.why_others_wrong: A nonsense mutation, by definition, typically has a very significant effect on protein length/function (via premature truncation), contrary to having no effect; a nonsense mutation can occur at various positions within a gene's coding sequence (not being restricted only to occurring at the very end), with its severity often depending on how early the premature stop codon occurs; a nonsense mutation specifically results in a SHORTENED (truncated), not lengthened, protein, since translation terminates prematurely.
solution.concept_recap: Nonsense mutations occurring early within a gene's coding sequence tend to be particularly disruptive, since a large portion of the intended protein is missing from the truncated product.

ncertRef: NCERT Class 12, Ch. 6 (Molecular Basis of Inheritance)

question: Which of the following best describes 'multiple alleles,' as illustrated by the ABO blood group system?
options: A situation in which more than two allelic forms of a gene exist within a population, though any individual diploid organism can carry at most two of these alleles
A situation in which a single individual can carry more than two alleles for a gene simultaneously
A term synonymous with polygenic inheritance
A phenomenon that has never been documented in any real gene

solution.why_correct: Multiple alleles describes a situation in which more than two allelic forms of a particular gene exist within a population as a whole (such as the three ABO alleles: IA, IB, and i); however, any single diploid individual can still carry at most two of these alleles at any given time (one on each homologous chromosome).
solution.why_others_wrong: A single individual carrying MORE than two alleles simultaneously would not be possible for a standard diploid organism at a single gene locus -- the key point of multiple alleles is population-level diversity, not individual-level excess; multiple alleles (many forms of ONE gene) and polygenic inheritance (multiple DIFFERENT genes affecting one trait) are distinct concepts, not being synonymous; multiple alleles have been well-documented in numerous real genes (the ABO system being a classic example), contrary to never being documented.
solution.concept_recap: The distinction between population-level allelic diversity (multiple alleles) and individual-level allele pairing (still only two per individual) is an important nuance in understanding this genetic concept.

question: Which of the following best describes why sex-linked traits (such as X-linked recessive conditions) often show different frequencies of occurrence between males and females in a population?
options: Sex-linked genes are located on the Y chromosome, which only males possess, so only males can be affected in any way

Males (XY) have only a single copy of most X-linked genes, so a single recessive allele is sufficient to cause the condition, whereas females (XX) generally require two copies (homozygous recessive) for the same condition to be expressed
Sex-linked traits show absolutely no difference in frequency between males and females
Sex-linked inheritance patterns have no relationship to the specific sex chromosomes involved

solution.why_correct: Since males (XY) possess only a single X chromosome, they have only one copy of most X-linked genes; a single recessive allele on this one X chromosome is therefore sufficient to cause an X-linked recessive condition, whereas females (XX), having two X chromosomes, generally require two copies of the recessive allele (homozygous recessive) for the same condition to be phenotypically expressed, since a single dominant allele on their other X chromosome would otherwise mask it.
solution.why_others_wrong: Most X-linked recessive conditions (like haemophilia, colour blindness) are located on the X chromosome (not the Y), and importantly, FEMALES CAN be affected too (though less commonly, requiring two recessive alleles), so it is not accurate that 'only males can be affected in any way'; X-linked traits characteristically DO show different frequencies between males and females (typically higher in males for X-linked recessive conditions), contrary to showing 'absolutely no difference'; sex-linked inheritance patterns have a very direct, defining relationship to the specific sex chromosomes involved (X or Y), contrary to having no such relationship.
solution.concept_recap: This differential frequency pattern (more males affected by X-linked recessive conditions) is a key diagnostic clue used in pedigree analysis to help identify X-linked recessive inheritance.

ncertRef: NCERT Class 12, Ch. 5 (Principles of Inheritance and Variation)

question: Which of the following best describes the overall flow of genetic information described by the 'central dogma' of molecular biology?
options: Protein to RNA to DNA
DNA to RNA to Protein
RNA to Protein to DNA, with no role for RNA in between
DNA directly to Protein, with no RNA intermediate involved at all

solution.why_correct: The central dogma of molecular biology describes the general flow of genetic information as DNA to RNA (via transcription) to Protein (via translation), representing the fundamental pathway by which genetic information stored in DNA is ultimately expressed as functional proteins.
solution.why_others_wrong: Protein to RNA to DNA reverses the correct, standard direction of information flow described by the central dogma; RNA to Protein to DNA also misrepresents the standard flow, incorrectly placing DNA at the end rather than the beginning; DNA generally does NOT go directly to protein without an RNA intermediate -- the RNA intermediate (via transcription) is a crucial, defining step in the standard central dogma pathway.
solution.concept_recap: While some exceptions exist (such as reverse transcription in certain retroviruses, going from RNA back to DNA), the standard DNA-to-RNA-to-protein flow remains the fundamental, general principle described by the central dogma.
